strengths: MSAM addresses a practically important problem with a simple implementation: reusing the momentum buffer permits one gradient evaluation per update without additional persistent optimizer state. Table 1 reports relative speed of 0.99 versus 0.52 for SAM, supporting the computational advantage.

The empirical improvements over base optimizers are meaningful across several architectures. Examples include 76.90% to 79.11% on CIFAR100 with WRN-16-4 and 67.0% to 69.1% on ImageNet with ViT-S/32. Compatibility with adaptive and BatchNorm-only perturbations, together with the matched-compute experiments in Appendix A.8, strengthens the practical contribution.

The extensive ablations provide useful insights beyond the proposed optimizer. Investigating perturbation sign, previous-gradient and random perturbations, curvature, and normalization helps identify the importance of separating perturbation magnitude from the learning-rate schedule.

The main algorithm is understandable, and the manuscript provides a code/configuration link, training details, hardware information, and extensive hyperparameter sweeps. The explicit discussion of warm-up sensitivity and instability is valuable transparency. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the described work.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantee is not established as written. Proposition 1 in Appendix A.1 is false for negative-trace Hessians: with a one-dimensional Hessian H = -1 and standard Gaussian perturbations with rho = 1, its left-hand side is approximately -0.199, while the claimed upper bound is -1. Setting 1 does not exclude negative trace. Theorem 3 also omits conditions needed to control Gaussian tails, Taylor remainders, and the relationship between unperturbed and perturbed population risk. Consequently, Section 4.1's assertion that improved generalization directly follows from this argument is unsupported.

The ImageNet comparison uses different warm-up treatments: MSAM perturbations are disabled during warm-up, whereas SAM perturbations remain active. Table A.2 shows that applying the same treatment improves SAM from 69.2% to 69.8%, exceeding MSAM's 69.1%. This disclosed result materially weakens the headline accuracy-parity claim; the principal comparisons should use matched scheduling and tuning opportunities.

Hyperparameter selection and statistical reliability remain insufficiently documented. Appendix A.15 reports the best rho alongside dense test-accuracy sweeps without specifying a separate validation-based selection protocol, leaving possible test-set selection bias unresolved. ImageNet configurations generally have only one run, and variability measured for smaller baseline models cannot establish uncertainty for different models and optimizers. The small translation differences likewise lack uncertainty estimates.

The claim of broadly preserving SAM's accuracy needs qualification. Table 2 shows substantial gaps for ViT-S/16 at 300 epochs, 75.8% versus 78.2%, and ViT-B/16 at 90 epochs, 75.7% versus 77.7%. The ImageNet matched-compute experiment covers only ViT-S/32. These results establish a promising speed–accuracy tradeoff, but do not yet establish comparable performance under equal budgets for the larger models where MSAM loses most accuracy.

Some mechanistic interpretations exceed the measurements. Section 4.2 projects the MSAM gradient into the plane spanned by SAM and SGD gradients; agreement after projection can hide an arbitrarily large orthogonal component and therefore does not establish full-gradient similarity. Moreover, Appendix A.2 finds normalization largely unnecessary, making independent lookahead scaling central to the contribution. A more precise distinction from existing NAG/extrapolation methods, supported by full-space gradient comparisons, would strengthen the originality and explanatory claims.
